content: Many studies on covert bacteriuria in children were conducted in the 1970s, but there is still uncertainty about whether treatment is beneficial because the results regarding treatment effectiveness are inconsistent. It is crucial to determine whether antibiotics or other treatments can effectively eliminate the infection, reduce recurrence, and prevent long-term kidney damage. Any potential benefits of treatment must outweigh the risks or harms to the individual child. This review aimed to assess the benefits and harms of treating covert bacteriuria in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE (from 1966), and EMBASE (from 1988) without language restrictions. The last search was performed on December 28, 2011. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that investigated interventions for covert bacteriuria in children up to 18 years of age. These children had culture-proven urinary tract infections (UTIs) but exhibited no urinary symptoms at the time of diagnosis. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data. Statistical analyses were conducted using a random-effects model, with results expressed as risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for dichotomous outcomes, and mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes. Three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 460 children (all girls) were included in the review. However, the methodological quality of these studies was generally weak, and gaps in reporting made it difficult to fully assess their reliability. One study found that the number of children with bacteriuria was significantly reduced six months after antibiotic treatment (RR 0.33; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.83). However, two studies reported no evidence of a reduction in persistent bacteriuria two years after treatment (RR 0.32; 95% CI 0.03 to 3.44). At follow-up four to five years after initial treatment, all included studies indicated that antibiotic treatment was effective in reducing the number of children with bacteriuria (RR 0.54; 95% CI 0.42 to 0.70). There were no significant differences in kidney growth between treated and untreated groups (MD 0.62; 95% CI -0.43 to 1.68). None of the studies provided data on treatment compliance or adverse effects. The authors concluded that the included studies do not provide sufficient evidence to draw reliable conclusions about the harms and benefits of treating covert bacteriuria in children. Based on the available data, antibiotic treatment for covert bacteriuria does not appear to provide long-term benefits for children.
